sections.body_en:
One of the difficult halakhic questions is the question of autopsies. Over the last two hundred years the medical profession has required operations to be performed on the dead. The first aim is the study of anatomy, that is, understanding the structure of the human body. For this purpose many operations were performed in which bodies were dissected into their parts, in order to examine the structure of the organs, the bones, the blood system and more. The second aim is the study of pathology, that is, knowledge of diseases and the ways they damage the body, and this, of course, in order to develop methods of healing. In addition, the medical schools required many dead bodies, so that medical students could practise on them operations that would afterwards be performed on living people.

And the question is whether, according to halakha, it is permitted to perform operations on the dead.

This question is very complex. Let us first preface: from a halakhic point of view there are several prohibitions involved in an autopsy. First, we are commanded to bury the dead and to accord him honour (as explained below 16:5), and certainly the operation disgraces him. The mitzva "You shall love your neighbour as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18) also requires us to treat him with honour (Amud Ha-Yemini 34). And if because of the operation his burial is delayed by a day, one thereby transgresses the prohibition "his body shall not remain overnight" (Devarim 21:23). In addition, there is a prohibition of deriving benefit from the body of the dead, and in the view of several poskim those who perform an autopsy transgress this prohibition (Ḥatam Sofer YD 336; and according to the Ḥazon Ish YD 208:7 there is no prohibition of benefit from the dead in an autopsy).

If so, it is clear that as a rule autopsies are not to be permitted. However, in a case where by the operation human life can be saved, it is permitted to operate on him, because pikuaḥ nefesh, that is, saving human life, overrides the whole Torah (Yoma 84b); and therefore in certain cases of pikuaḥ nefesh one may be lenient and perform autopsies.

We have learned that according to the Torah there is a prohibition against performing an autopsy, because it involves disgrace to the dead, delay of burial, and several other prohibitions.

Now let us clarify what the law is in a case of pikuaḥ nefesh. For example, what will the law be in a case where two patients fell ill with the same disease, and the strength of one did not hold out and he died, and the second patient remains before us in a situation of mortal danger? Is the doctor permitted in such a case to operate on the body of the patient who died, in order to determine the exact nature of that disease, and thereby perhaps be able to save the life of the second patient?

The important posek Rabbi Yeḥezkel Landau, rabbi of Prague more than two hundred years ago, wrote about this in his famous book "Noda Bi-Yehuda" (part 2, YD 210) that although there is a prohibition against performing an autopsy, nevertheless we hold the rule: pikuaḥ nefesh overrides all the mitzvot (Yoma 84b), and therefore, in order to save the second patient, it is permitted to perform the autopsy.

Admittedly, there was one who disagreed with this ruling, because in his view a person who has died is exempt from all the mitzvot, and he no longer has a mitzva to save his fellow's life; therefore it is forbidden to disgrace him and operate on him. And although we have a halakha that a person is permitted to steal bread or money in order to save his life, nevertheless this is specifically on condition that afterwards he tries to return what he stole. But in the case of the dead, since it is not possible to compensate him for the disgrace caused to him, it is forbidden to disgrace him even for the sake of saving life (Binyan Tziyon part 1, 170-171).

But in halakha it has been ruled, by almost all the poskim, that it is permitted to perform an autopsy in order to save human life. For pikuaḥ nefesh overrides all the mitzvot of the Torah, including the mitzva to honour the dead. And so ruled the Ḥatam Sofer (YD 336), the Maharam Schick (YD 347-348), the Tzitz Eliezer (part 4, 14), and many others. And all this of course on condition that everything is done with maximum consideration for the honour of the dead, and that after the operation he is buried whole.

sections.title_en: 3. Autopsies for the Sake of Patients Who Are Not Before Us
sections.body_en:
With the development of medicine and the discovery of new drugs, the question arose whether it is permitted to operate on patients who died of serious diseases, such as cancer, AIDS, heart disease and the like, in order to find ways of curing those diseases. For example, sometimes a new drug against cancer is tried, and in the end the patient dies, and they want to check how the drug affected him. For this purpose his body must be operated on. This examination can have an immediate effect: if on the basis of several examinations of patients who died they see that the effect of the drug is negative, they can immediately stop its use; and if they see that the effect of the drug is positive, they can increase its use. The question is whether it is permitted to perform autopsies for this purpose.

Several poskim wrote that it is possible that in the view of the author of the Noda Bi-Yehuda it is forbidden to perform autopsies for the sake of discovering drugs. For the whole permission of the Noda Bi-Yehuda to perform autopsies is only for the sake of a dangerously ill patient who is now before us; only in such a case does pikuaḥ nefesh override the prohibition of disgracing the dead. But for the sake of patients who are in other hospitals and of whose existence we do not know, it is forbidden.

But in the view of many poskim, in the case of common diseases, even when there is no dangerously ill patient in that hospital, it is permitted to perform autopsies. For it is clear to us that in other hospitals there are at this time patients suffering from the same disease, and since today it is possible to announce immediately the discovery of a new drug, all the patients with that disease are considered as being before us, and for the sake of saving them it is permitted to perform an autopsy (Ḥazon Ish YD 208:7; Tzitz Eliezer 4:14; Rabbi Goren; Rabbi Weinberg, Teḥumin 12, 382).

It is important to note that many times it has happened that doctors claimed that there was a need of pikuaḥ nefesh to perform an autopsy, whereas religious doctors of name and reputation claimed that there was no necessity at all for it. Therefore it is clear that in this matter one can rely only on God-fearing doctors who understand the value of the honour of the dead. And if such doctors say that there is a need to perform an autopsy in order to save human life, it is permitted – and in the view of most poskim even a mitzva – to listen to them and agree to the autopsy.

sections.title_en: 4. Autopsies for the Sake of Patients Who Will Appear in the Future
sections.body_en:
We have learned that although there is a Torah prohibition against performing autopsies, if the operation is done in order to discover ways of saving dangerously ill patients suffering from the same disease, it is permitted, because of pikuaḥ nefesh; that is, saving the lives of dangerously ill patients overrides the prohibition of performing an autopsy. All this is on condition that through this operation the life of a patient who is suffering right now, at the time the autopsy is performed, from the same disease may be saved.

But the question is whether it is permitted to perform autopsies in order to save by them patients who will appear in the future. For example, the research involved will take a long time more, and it is clear that the results of the present autopsy will not be able to help save people who are already in danger now. Or, for example, when a new and dangerous disease begins to appear in the world, which is not yet common, and therefore it is not clear whether in the other hospitals in the country there are patients suffering from it. And the doctors want to research the disease and the ways of curing it, in order to learn how to cure patients who may appear in the future. The question is whether such a need too permits an autopsy.

In such a case there is a dispute.

In the view of Rabbi Feinstein, if at present no other patients suffering from that disease are known to us, it is forbidden to perform autopsies in order to save patients who may perhaps appear in the future. And even if there are before us patients suffering from that disease, but it is clear that the autopsies performed now will not help them, because the research will take a long time and in the meantime those patients before us will die – in this case too it is forbidden to perform an autopsy. The reason for this is that according to this view, the rule of pikuaḥ nefesh applies only when it is a matter of saving a person who is before us now. But for the sake of rescue from dangers that may perhaps appear in the future, it is forbidden to transgress the mitzvot of the Torah (Igrot Moshe YD 2:151). And so it is implied from the words of the Noda Bi-Yehuda (part 2, YD 210).

But in the view of the author of the Ḥazon Ish, it makes no difference whether there is at present in one of the hospitals a patient suffering from that disease; rather, everything depends on the degree of likelihood that the disease will spread in the future. If there is a concern that the disease will spread, it is permitted to perform autopsies on people who died of it, in order to learn how to cure people who may fall ill with it in the future (Ḥazon Ish YD 208:7).

And Rabbi Goren added that even in the view of the Noda Bi-Yehuda it would be permitted. For all that the Noda Bi-Yehuda wrote, that it is forbidden to perform an autopsy for the sake of a patient who may perhaps appear in the future, refers specifically to a private doctor who is not connected to a large medical organisation, like the doctors two hundred years ago. Such a doctor is forbidden to perform an autopsy so that perhaps he will be able to save such a patient if he comes before him in the future. But the medical institutions in the State of Israel have responsibility for millions of Jews, and therefore it is incumbent on them to take into account future patients too, and this is considered pikuaḥ nefesh. Therefore it is permitted to perform autopsies if thereby they can find ways of curing patients in the future (Rabbi Weinberg also wrote similarly, Teḥumin 12, 382).

And again it is important to emphasise that experience proves that in this matter one can rely only on God-fearing doctors. Only they are trusted to say that there is indeed a need to perform the autopsy because of pikuaḥ nefesh.

It is further important to note that in practice, only in a few cases is there today a real need to perform autopsies in order to invent drugs for future diseases. For generally, by examinations that do not require an operation, almost everything can be known. And such examinations may be performed even according to the stringent view. For example, according to all views it is permitted to insert a needle into the dead and draw from him a little blood or tissue, and likewise it is permitted to insert an instrument into the body of the dead in order to see through it what is happening in the cavity of his body. And after these examinations, in the great majority of cases, there is no longer any need to perform an operation (Igrot Moshe YD 2:151).

sections.title_en: 5. Autopsies for the Study of Anatomy and Pathology
sections.body_en:
Over the last two hundred years medical science has developed to a great extent through autopsies. Through the operations the field of anatomy developed, that is, knowledge of the human body with all its organs, arteries and sinews. Operating on the dead who had been ill developed the field of pathology, that is, the study of diseases. And the branch of surgery too developed through this. In practice, for decades it was the custom in Israel and in Western countries to perform autopsies on half the patients who died in hospitals.

And since there is a Torah prohibition against disgracing the dead and damaging his body, a difficult question arose: is it permitted to perform autopsies for the sake of developing medical science and training surgeons?

In the view of the great majority of poskim, it is forbidden to study anatomy through autopsies. And although we hold the rule that pikuaḥ nefesh overrides all the mitzvot of the Torah, including the prohibition against performing autopsies, nevertheless this is specifically in rare cases in which the doctors hold that through this operation they will discover new things about the disease, and thereby they will be able to save people from death. But to perform autopsies on half the dead wholesale, as was the custom, is something unthinkable. Admittedly pikuaḥ nefesh overrides the mitzvot, but it does not abolish them. Therefore the whole permission to perform autopsies can be carried out only in special cases, in which there is a reasonable chance that through the operation human life can be saved. But to teach medical students anatomy through autopsies is forbidden, because they can be taught by means of imaging, and there is no need to disgrace the dead for this. (Admittedly, Responsa Mishpetei Uziel YD 28-29 permitted it, since this too is considered a need of pikuaḥ nefesh; but as stated, to the extent that a substitute for autopsies can be found, it is reasonable that even in his view it is forbidden.)

And if a person comes and asks: but in order to advance in the fields of anatomy and pathology one must perform autopsies on many dead – one can answer him that in these fields the gentiles will advance, for whom there is no prohibition against performing autopsies. But we are permitted to perform an autopsy only for a special need of pikuaḥ nefesh. And so Rav Kook wrote, that one should not take bodies of Jews for the purpose of medical study. And in a case of necessity, one should buy bodies of gentiles, because among the Jewish people the sanctity of the body has special importance, and for this the Jewish people agreed to take upon itself many prohibitions, among them the prohibition of eating forbidden foods. And although the haters of Israel will not understand this, the good among the nations of the world will understand that we cannot perform autopsies on the Jewish dead for the sake of medical study and the advancement of the science of anatomy (Da'at Kohen 199).[1]

notes_en.en: Admittedly, it is reasonable that if there were a situation in which there was no possibility of relying on autopsies of gentiles, or on the discoveries made abroad, and in the view of the doctors they would have to perform several autopsies in order to advance medicine and the ability to save patients, it is reasonable that the law would change, and most poskim would permit autopsies because of pikuaḥ nefesh; and so ruled Mishpetei Uziel, Maḥane Ḥayim YD part 2, 60, Yaskil Avdi part 6, YD 19.

sections.body_en:
Throughout the Western world, for decades it was the custom to perform autopsies on about half the patients who died in hospitals, on the claim that these operations are carried out for the sake of saving lives, for by them one checks whether the doctors were right in their diagnosis. And likewise it is possible that in one of the operations something new will be discovered by which human life can be saved. And further, through the operations medical students are accustomed and trained in the work of surgery.

Admittedly, according to halakha there is no prohibition against performing autopsies on gentile dead; but it is clear that the great majority of the autopsies performed on Jewish dead were done unlawfully, and they transgressed by them the prohibitions of disgracing the dead, delaying burial and deriving benefit from the dead.

Let us now address a number of arguments that were voiced in favour of autopsies.

It was argued that through a post-mortem operation the doctors will be able to know whether they diagnosed correctly, and thereby they will be able to improve their treatment of other patients. One could take this argument into account if the treating doctors took part in the operation, or at least received precise results from them. But in practice the doctors receive, very late, general and vague answers that give them no benefit (see Assia 1, 212 and Assia 6, 290).

A further reason was voiced in favour of autopsies: that through them students practise the work of surgery, and thereby, when they operate on patients, they will be more successful in their work. But pikuaḥ nefesh can override the mitzva of honouring the dead only when there is no choice, and since it is possible to practise in another way too, by means of imaging, there is no permission to disgrace the dead for the sake of practising surgery.

A further argument that was voiced: perhaps in one of tens or hundreds of thousands of operations something new will be discovered by which human life will be saved. Such a chance cannot in any way be considered pikuaḥ nefesh. For if we treated the concern of pikuaḥ nefesh with such stringency, we would have to forbid people to travel in cars for fear of accidents, and likewise we would permit a pharmaceutical factory to produce on Shabbat, lest suddenly many patients come who will need the drugs. And likewise we would have to permit weapons factories to work on Shabbat, and soldiers to train on Shabbat, even when there is no likelihood of an imminent war, lest a war nevertheless suddenly break out. And not only this, but if we were so concerned about pikuaḥ nefesh, we would have to oblige people to accumulate money, so that if poor people who may die come their way, they will be able to save them. And likewise we would oblige all people to study medicine, lest one day a sick person come before them and there be no one who can treat him (see Noda Bi-Yehuda part 2, YD 210; Igrot Moshe YD part 2, 151).

Rather, it is clear that normal life cannot be harmed by an exaggerated concern for pikuaḥ nefesh. And likewise it is not possible to abolish the mitzva of honouring the dead because of the remote chance that perhaps, perhaps, through his autopsy another person's life will be saved. Rather, the rule is that pikuaḥ nefesh overrides the mitzvot of the Torah only in a case where there is a reasonable and near concern of danger, and by our transgressing one of the mitzvot there is a reasonable chance of rescue. But in a situation where only in one of several thousand autopsies new things will perhaps be discovered, it is not possible, for the sake of that single case, to permit the dissection and disgrace of the bodies of thousands of dead.

One of the central questions in the matter of autopsies is what the standing of the family members is. On the one hand, it is clear that the relatives have no ownership of the body of their relative, and therefore they have no permission to sell or donate his body to science. And if the relatives disgrace his body, the mitzva falls on the public to see to his honourable burial.

On the other hand, the question is asked: in a case where there is a need of pikuaḥ nefesh to perform an autopsy on the body, for example in order to discover through it a cure for a dangerous disease, can the operation be carried out against the position of the family members?

In the view of most poskim, even for the sake of pikuaḥ nefesh it is forbidden to perform an autopsy on the body without the family's permission. The reason is that since he is in their charge, the duty to bury him with honour is theirs, and if he is disgraced, they too are disgraced with him. Therefore a person who instructed in his lifetime that they should not bury him – one does not listen to his instruction, and one buries him, because the matter concerns his relatives too, who will be disgraced if he is not buried (Rabbi Arieli, No'am 6, section 14; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:9). And just as one cannot force a person to donate his money for the sake of saving his fellow, so one cannot oblige them to disgrace themselves for the sake of saving another person. However, since it is a matter of an operation for the sake of saving life, several rabbis ruled that it is a mitzva to persuade the family members to agree. But if they refuse, one should not operate on him without their permission (Rabbi Soloveitchik, Assia 1, 227; Rabbi Goren).[2]

One of the most negative laws that existed in the country concerned autopsies. Until the year 5741, doctors were permitted to perform autopsies without the consent of the family members. The condition was that three doctors sign that there was a need for it in order to determine the cause of death, or in order to use part of the body for healing another person. And so there were many cases in which, out of contempt for the honour of the dead, doctors signed forms without examining the case, until they reached a situation in which half of those who died in hospitals were operated on after their death – a percentage that certainly far exceeds anything that can be permitted for the sake of pikuaḥ nefesh. It is impossible to describe the terrible distress of the family of the deceased when it became clear to them that the body of their loved one had been dissected, and even that organs had been taken from it for research. Many people feared dying in hospitals for fear that their bodies would be operated on after their death. And when a person from a religious family died in hospital, the family members would immediately organise a guard beside his body, and strive to prevent his autopsy by force.

After the Likud came to power, in the year 5741, the law was amended and it was established that without the consent of the family members it is forbidden to perform an operation on the dead to determine the cause of death. And if it is a matter of taking an organ in order to save another's life, it is permitted to do so without asking the family, on condition that a reasonable attempt is made to inform them of it; but if the family expressed opposition, even for the sake of saving another, it is forbidden to perform an autopsy (Encyclopedia Hilkhatit Refu'it 4, pp. 536-540 and 586-587).

notes_en.en: Admittedly, there is one who wrote that where there is pikuaḥ nefesh, one does not listen to the family members (Yaskil Avdi part 6, YD 19). And it is possible that in special cases in which there is a very high likelihood that through the operation human life will be saved, one may rely as a temporary ruling on the words of those who permit, and perform the autopsy against the family's wishes, on condition that a responsible committee of doctors and rabbis decides on it.

sections.body_en:
Question: In recent generations, with the development of medical science, there are people who donate their bodies to science, so that anatomy and pathology can be studied on their bodies. According to halakha, is it fitting to donate one's body to science?

Answer: According to halakha there is a mitzva to honour the body of the dead and to bury it with the greatest speed. The disgrace of performing an autopsy is not only to the dead himself, but also to his family, and even to all Israel. For a Divine soul dwells in each and every Jew, and therefore we were commanded to honour the body of the dead in which the Divine soul dwelt. And so it is clear that it is forbidden to donate the body to science, because thereby the burial will be delayed and the body will be disgraced. Admittedly, pikuaḥ nefesh overrides the prohibition of disgracing the dead, and therefore in special cases, where through the operation human life can be saved, it is permitted to perform an autopsy. But all this is only in a case of special need. But one who donates his body to science allows it to be operated on even not for the sake of pikuaḥ nefesh, and therefore it is forbidden. And it is fitting to note here that this law is particular to Israel, who were commanded in several mitzvot to sanctify and honour the body; but a gentile who donates his body to science – it will be accounted to him as a trait of piety (Da'at Kohen 199).

A further question that should be clarified is: what is the law if a person nevertheless went ahead and donated his body to science – according to halakha does his instruction have validity or not?

Answer: Donating the body has two meanings. The first is cancelling or delaying the burial, for example, they will keep his skeleton for years in a museum, and examine other organs for several weeks. And the second is the consent that they operate on the body and examine all its parts.

Regarding burial, it is a settled halakha in the Rambam that even if a person instructed that they should not bury him, one does not listen to him, because there is in this a disgrace to the family and to all Israel. Therefore a person's consent to the cancellation of burial, or even to its postponement, is of no effect at all (Laws of Mourning 12:1; Amud Ha-Yemini 34:5).

But regarding consent to an operation on the body, when immediately afterwards it will be buried, the poskim disagreed.

In the view of most poskim, even the person himself has no right to permit the disgrace of his body, because the prohibition derives from the fact that man was created in the image of God, and the Divine soul rested in this body for years. Therefore we were commanded to treat the body of the dead with honour, and not to derive benefit from it, and not to use it for the study of anatomy, pathology and surgery. And so ruled the Ḥatam Sofer (YD 336), the Maharam Schick (YD 347), Rav Kook (Da'at Kohen 199), and Rabbi Feinstein (Igrot Moshe YD 3:140).

But in the view of several poskim, it is permitted to perform an autopsy on the body of a person who agreed to it in his lifetime. Their reason is that the whole basis of the prohibition of disgracing the body of the dead is so as not to harm his honour; but if he himself agreed that they operate on him, then there is no longer a prohibition to operate on him. And so ruled Responsa Binyan Tziyon (170), and the Tzitz Eliezer (4:14). And the Council of the Chief Rabbinate too, in the period of Rabbi Herzog, determined that it had no objection to autopsies on the dead who agreed to it in their lifetime, because the doctors may rely in this on the view of those who permit (Encyclopedia Hilkhatit Refu'it 4, 537).

It is important to repeat and emphasise that the whole permission according to the lenient view is only regarding the autopsy, but it is forbidden to postpone the burial for this even by one day.[3]

notes_en.en: In the view of Rabbi Yisraeli ztz"l in his book Amud Ha-Yemini 34, the mitzva of burial applies to the majority of the body, and therefore in a case where the deceased agreed to it, it is permitted to delay the burial of individual organs for a number of days, but the majority of the body must be buried immediately on that same day. And in the view of Rabbi Waldenberg in Responsa Tzitz Eliezer 4:14, all the parts of the body must be buried on that same day.

sections.title_en: 9. An Autopsy to Incriminate a Murderer and to Free an Aguna
sections.body_en:
Question: Sometimes when a person is murdered, the police demand that his body be operated on so that thereby they can find his murderer, incriminate him and punish him. In such a case can one be lenient and perform an autopsy?

Rabbi Klatzkin of Lublin answered about this in his book "Imrei Shefer" (siman 82) that in order to find the murderer and punish him, it is permitted to perform an autopsy on the body of the murdered person. And those relatives who try to prevent the operation act wrongly, and thereby cause the murder to be concealed and prevent the possibility of punishing the murderer at trial. For the whole prohibition of performing an autopsy is so as not to harm his honour, but in such a case the murdered person certainly waives his honour provided that his murderer is punished. And although there is one who was stringent (Responsa Ḥemdat Tzvi part 2, YD 20), nevertheless this is the view of most poskim, and so ruled the Tzitz Eliezer (part 4, 14:9), and Rabbi Tukachinsky in his book "Gesher Ha-Ḥayim" (part 2, chapter 28:2).

A further question came before the poskim on this subject: what is the law when a person died far from his home, and they did not know who he was, and buried him? And it is possible that he is the husband of a certain woman, and as long as no witnesses are found who saw that he indeed died, his wife will remain in a state of aguna, having no husband and also unable to marry. In such a case, in order to free her from her state of aguna, will it be permitted to open the grave of the deceased whose name was not known, in order to check whether this is her husband?

The well-known posek, the author of the responsa "Sho'el U-Meshiv" (Mahadura Kamma part 1, 231), permitted opening the grave in order to free her from her state of aguna. For when it is a matter of so great a need as freeing an aguna, it is clear that opening the grave is not intended to disgrace him, but only to save his wife from her chains. And although some were stringent (Pitḥei Teshuva YD 363:7, based on Shivat Tziyon 64, and Teshuva Me-Ahava 47-48), nevertheless the view of most poskim is to be lenient (Rabbi Y. Arieli, Torah She-Be'al Peh 6; Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Nishmat Avraham YD 349:1).

sections.title_en: 10. An Autopsy for the Sake of Receiving Insurance Money
sections.body_en:
It happened that a person who had paid for years for life insurance overturned with his car and fell into a river, drowned and died. In the insurance agreement it was stated that if the death was caused by an accident, the family members would be entitled to double payment from the insurance company. And indeed the family members claimed that the death was caused by an accident. But against them, the insurance company claimed that the death was caused by a heart attack, and only afterwards did the car overturn and fall into the river; and as long as it is not proven that he did not suffer a heart attack, the insurance company will not pay the double payment. Is the family permitted to agree that the body of the deceased be operated on in order to check whether he suffered a heart attack, or must they give up the double payment, provided that the body of their loved one is not disgraced?

Several poskim disagreed about this. Some ruled that since the deceased paid for insurance for years, it is clear that his wish was that his family members receive compensation after his death, and therefore the family members are permitted to agree that he be operated on. All the more so since the deceased himself signed the contract, which included a clause allowing the insurance company to demand a post-mortem operation. And admittedly, if the family members had demanded that he be operated on, there might have been room to be stringent; but when the insurance company initiates the request for the post-mortem operation, the family members have no duty to refuse and thereby lose their claim.

But against them, several poskim ruled that since a special mitzva rests on the family members to honour the dead and to see to it that he is not disgraced, they are forbidden to agree that his body be operated on. And although we find in the Talmud (Bava Batra 154a) that sometimes because of a monetary claim it is permitted to examine the body of the dead, nevertheless there the matter is a slight disgrace, that is, an external look at his body before burial, and even this was permitted only for those who are not his relatives. But here, where it is a matter of the great disgrace of operating on the body for the sake of the relatives, it is forbidden, and the family members are obligated to oppose the post-mortem operation even if thereby they lose the insurance payment (Ha-Bitu'aḥ Ba-Halakha 127-135).

And in any case it is clear that this problem should be prevented at its root, and therefore every Jew who wishes to insure himself with life insurance must demand of the insurance company that it omit from his policy the clause allowing the company to demand a post-mortem operation. And so he will guard his honour and prevent distress to his family (Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:85, in the note).[4]

notes_en.en: If it is possible to carry out this examination without causing great disgrace, for example by inserting a needle to draw a little material from the heart (biopsy), it appears that one may be more lenient; see Igrot Moshe YD part 2, 151.
